reading.title: Comparing vehicles and destinations
reading.text: At a space-center exhibition, Sami compares machines with the worlds they explore. A rocket produces thrust to carry a vehicle or payload. NASA's historical space shuttle used a winged orbiter within a partly reusable system. An artificial satellite operates in space; a capsule can carry crew or cargo. A lander reaches a surface, while a rover travels over it. A probe investigates a destination without a crew. A booster supplies additional launch thrust. Payload means carried equipment or cargo, and launch pad is the launch platform. The Sun is a star. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the four inner planets in that order. Sami separates a machine's purpose from its destination. A model's size does not represent actual planetary distances unless a stated scale is used.

reading.title: Following a mission description
reading.text: Sami reads a mission description before interpreting the display. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Saturn has an extensive ring system, and the other giant planets also have rings. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. An asteroid is a small rocky or metallic body; a comet contains ice and other material. An astronaut is trained for spaceflight. A spacesuit supports the wearer in the conditions for which it is designed, and a helmet protects the head as part of the system. Mission control supports a mission from the ground. Countdown precedes the event; liftoff begins ascent, orbit names a curved path around another body, and spacewalk names activity outside a spacecraft. The description supplies facts that a generic model cannot prove.

reading.title: Describing operations and observations
reading.text: The exhibition separates mission operations from astronomical phenomena. Docking joins spacecraft. Re-entry returns a vehicle into an atmosphere; splashdown lands it in water. A telescope observes distant objects. A star produces energy, and a galaxy is a vast gravitationally related system containing stars and other matter. A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust. A black hole has an event horizon from within which light cannot escape. A supernova is a stellar explosion, while a constellation is a named pattern or sky region as viewed from Earth. Meteor describes the luminous atmospheric streak. Aurora concerns light from interactions involving charged particles and an atmosphere. An eclipse blocks light through alignment; cosmic dust names small solid grains. A solar panel converts light into electricity. Sami asks whether an image is an observation, model or illustration.
reading.imageBrief: Support for Describing operations and observations. Reuse independently reviewed word references; the text supplies historical, technical or personal facts.

reading.title: Comparing spacecraft subsystems
reading.text: Sami examines a generic spacecraft cutaway. An antenna sends or receives radio signals; radar uses radio waves to detect or measure objects. A computer processes information. A fuel tank stores fuel, while a thruster provides force to adjust motion or orientation. A heat shield protects against heating during atmospheric entry. A parachute slows descent where an atmosphere permits it. A robotic arm handles objects, and a laboratory provides equipment for investigations. The guide asks Sami to compare functions rather than infer performance from the model. The cutaway illustrates relationships but does not show every mission's design. A solar-powered system still needs suitable power management, and a shield's appearance does not establish its temperature limits. Engineering specifications and measurements support those claims.
